Text_Reference: Introduction section: 'We report a water-based optical clearing agent, SeeDB, which clears fixed brain samples in a few days without quenching many types of fluorescent dyes, including fluorescent proteins and lipophilic neuronal tracers.'

RESULTS section, 'SeeDB, an optical clearing agent using fructose and thiol': 'Together, these findings led us to establish the clearing agent SeeDB, which is a saturated solution of fructose (80.2% wt/wt) in water with 0.5% α-thioglycerol.'

General_Description.Text: SeeDB is a water-based optical clearing agent that clears fixed brain samples in a few days without quenching many types of fluorescent dyes, including fluorescent proteins and lipophilic neuronal tracers. This method maintains a constant sample volume during the clearing procedure, which is important for preserving cellular morphology, and facilitates the quantitative reconstruction of neuronal circuits. SeeDB allows imaging of the mouse brain from the dorsal to the ventral side, making it useful for imaging intact morphological architecture at large scales in both adult and developing brains.

Tissue_Types.Text3: SeeDB was applied to paraformaldehyde-fixed embryo and brain samples.
Text3_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Fine morphological architecture is preserved with SeeDB': 'We treated paraformaldehyde-fixed embryo and brain samples with increasing concentrations of aqueous fructose solutions and finally equilibrated them in SeeDB.'

Time_Consumption.Text1: The entire SeeDB clearing paraformaldehyde-fixed embryo and brain samples took approximately 3 days.
Text1_Reference: RESULTS section: 'We treated paraformaldehyde-fixed embryo and brain samples with increasing concentrations of aqueous fructose solutions and finally equilibrated them in SeeDB (Fig. 1). The entire procedure took approximately 3 d, whereas clearing with ScaleA2 took approximately 3 weeks to clear the mouse brain (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3)12.'

Tissue_Deformation.Text1: A key feature of SeeDB is that it maintains a constant sample volume during clearing, which preserves fine cellular morphology. Unlike methods that cause significant shrinkage (e.g., BABB, ~50%) or expansion (e.g., ScaleA2, 150%), SeeDB treatment results in dendritic morphology indistinguishable from the in vivo state.
Text1_Reference: Abstract: 'Our method maintained a constant sample volume during the clearing procedure, an important factor for keeping cellular morphology intact...'

RESULTS, 'Fine morphological architecture is preserved with SeeDB': '...optical clearing by BABB resulted in sample shrinkage...whereas optical clearing by ScaleA2 caused a 150% linear expansion in sample size.'
Results Section: 'In contrast, such morphological deformations were not observed in SeeDB-treated samples; the morphology of dendrites remained indistinguishable from those in vivo'

Fluorescence_Compatibility.Text2: The method is compatible with multiple fluorescent proteins for multi-color imaging, including EYFP, EGFP, and tdTomato.
Text2_Reference: RESULTS section: '...fluorescence of cytosolic EYFP was best preserved using SeeDB.'
Results Section: 'By introducing tdTomato and EGFP expression vectors to anterior and posterior regions, respectively, we were able to observe topographic organization of the corpus callosum'

Fluorescence_Compatibility.Text4: SeeDB was able to clear brain samples labeled with lipophilic dyes such as DiI, a powerful and commonly used neuronal tracer, because the plasma membrane remains intact.
Text4_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Fine morphological architecture is preserved with SeeDB': 'Furthermore, SeeDB was able to clear brain samples labeled with lipophilic dyes such as DiI, a powerful and commonly used neuronal tracer, because the plasma membrane remains intact.'

Fluorescence_Compatibility.Text1: SeeDB is compatible with fluorescent dextran tracers for labeling neuronal structures. Specific examples used include dextran-conjugated Alexa Fluor 488 (for in vivo imaging) and Alexa Fluor 647 (for post-fixation imaging).

Preservation_Stability.Text2: A comparison of various clearing agents using Thy1-YFP line G transgenic mice revealed that fluorescence of cytosolic EYFP was best preserved using SeeDB.
Text2_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Fine morphological architecture is preserved with SeeDB section': 'Unlike previous clearing agents, SeeDB does not change the chemical nature of the samples. For example, a comparison of various clearing agents using Thy1-YFP line G transgenic mice revealed that fluorescence of cytosolic EYFP was best preserved using SeeDB (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 6).'

Preservation_Stability.Text4: Samples can be stored in SeeDB (at 25 °C) or SeeDB37 (at 37 °C) for up to 1 week.
Text4_Reference: METHODS section: 'Samples can be stored in SeeDB (at 25 °C) or SeeDB37 (at 37 °C) for up to 1 week.'

Application.Text2: SeeDB facilitates imaging of intact morphological architecture at large scales in both the adult and developing brains.
Text2_Reference: ABSTRACT section: 'Our simple and efficient method is useful for imaging intact morphological architecture at large scales in both the adult and developing brains.'

Application.Text3: SeeDB enables imaging of the mouse brain from the dorsal to the ventral side using two-photon microscopy and an optimized objective lens.
Text3_Reference: ABSTRACT section: 'Combined with two-photon microscopy and an optimized objective lens, we were able to image the mouse brain from the dorsal to the ventral side.'

Application.Text4: SeeDB is particularly advantageous for quantitative analyses of fine neuronal morphology and microcircuits.
Text4_Reference: DISCUSSION section: 'SeeDB is particularly advantageous for quantitative analyses of fine neuronal morphology and microcircuits because minimal deformation artifacts occur during the clearing process.'

Application.Text5: Optical clearing with SeeDB was reversible and could also be combined with immunohistochemistry without loss of antigenicity.
Text5_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Fine morphological architecture is preserved with SeeDB': 'Optical clearing with SeeDB was reversible and could also be combined with immunohistochemistry without loss of antigenicity.'

Application.Text1: An application of SeeDB is the evaluation of its impact on fine neuronal morphology, demonstrated by imaging fluorescently labeled mitral cells in the olfactory bulb to assess the preservation of dendritic structures after clearing.
Text1_Reference: Results Section: 'To evaluate the changes to morphology resulting from optical clearing, we sparsely labeled a population of mitral cells in the olfactory bulb using fluorescent dextran tracers.'

Application.Text2: SeeDB is applied in developmental neurobiology for visualizing long-range axonal projections in neonatal brains. A specific example is the visualization of callosal axon projections between hemispheres in a whole-mount P7 mouse brain, where neurons were labeled with EGFP via in utero electroporation.
Text2_Reference: Results Section: 'SeeDB can be a powerful tool in developmental studies of embryonic and neonatal brains because of the minimal fragility and morphological damages to tissues.'

Results Section: 'For example, we were able to visualize long-range callosal axon projections from one hemisphere to the other using whole-mount P7 mouse brain samples (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Video 11). These mice had EGFP expression vectors introduced into layer II/III neurons...via in utero electroporation.'

Application.Text3: The SeeDB method was applied to the quantitative reconstruction of brain microcircuits within the olfactory bulb. The objective was to examine the diversity of inhibitory modulations via lateral dendrites among 'sister' mitral cells, an aspect for which the anatomical basis was previously unknown.
Text3_Reference: Results Section: 'SeeDB is also ideal for use in comprehensive and quantitative reconstruction of microcircuits in the brain.'

Results Section: 'We used our clearing method to examine the anatomical bases for odor information processing in a single glomerular module in the olfactory bulb... however, the extent of the diversity in the inhibitory modulations via lateral dendrites among sister mitral cells remains unknown'

Application.Text4: The SeeDB method was applied to overcome the limitations of mechanical sectioning in neuroanatomy. Factual achievements included: (1) Visualizing the near-complete wiring diagram of mitral cell dendrites from a whole-mount olfactory bulb sample. (2) Performing quantitative analysis of dendritic parameters from the 3D tracing data. (3) The quantification determined that the dendritic coverage areas of 'sister' mitral cells have minimal overlap (mean ± s.d. = 37 ± 30%), supporting the conclusion that they connect to highly diverse sets of synaptic partners.
Text4_Reference: Results Section: '...after optical clearing of this sample with SeeDB, we were able to visualize the near-complete wiring diagram of mitral cell dendrites using confocal microscopy (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Video 14).'
Results Section: 'On the basis of this tracing data, we quantified various parameters of mitral cell dendrites (Supplementary Table 2).'

Results Section: '...we found that the coverage areas of sister mitral cells only have small overlapping areas (mean ± s.d. = 37 ± 30%, n = 144 pairs; Fig. 6b and Supplementary Table 3)... Thus, our results support the idea that synaptic partners (granule cells) are highly diverse among sister mitral cells.'

Note.Text2: Longer incubation periods in the fructose solution (>7 d), especially at higher temperatures (for example, 37 °C), caused browning and autofluorescence accumulation as a result of the Maillard reaction.
Text2_Reference: RESULTS section, SeeDB, an optical clearing agent using fructose and thiol: 'Although longer incubation periods in the fructose solution (>7 d), especially at higher temperatures (for example, 37 °C), caused browning and autofluorescence accumulation as a result of the Maillard reaction, these effects could be avoided by adding thiols such as β-mercaptoethanol or α-thioglycerol to the solution.'

Note.Text5: Scale-treated samples are very fragile and difficult to handle because urea causes partial denaturation and loss of cellular proteins.
Text5_Reference: INTRODUCTION: 'Furthermore, because urea causes partial denaturation and loss of cellular proteins, the Scale-treated samples are very fragile and difficult to handle.'

Note.Text1: A noted limitation of SeeDB is its difficulty in clearing large tissue pieces, such as a full adult mouse brain, due to limited reagent permeability. While incubating at higher temperatures (e.g., 50 °C) can partially overcome this, it may cause some quenching of fluorescent proteins. Younger, smaller samples (e.g., P21 mouse brains) are easier to clear.
Text1_Reference: Results Section: 'As a result of the limited permeability of SeeDB, large pieces of tissue, such as the full brain of adult mice, were admittedly relatively difficult to clear.'

Results Section: 'This issue could be partly overcome by incubating samples at higher temperatures (for example, 50 °C), although this caused partial quenching of fluorescent proteins (SeeDB37ht; Online Methods and Supplementary Fig. 5a).'
Results Section: 'Brain samples of younger mice (for example, P21) were easier to clear using standard protocols'
